claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in the HEA is controlled by stress-assisted cyclic breakdown and reformation of a protective oxide film.
Mechanical sliding intermittently removes the passivating oxide layer.
Removal of the oxide exposes fresh reactive metal.
Cr and/or Al promote rapid re-oxidation of the exposed HEA surface.
The balance between oxide-removal and oxide-reformation rates governs the coupled wear-corrosion response.
The as-fabricated HEA initially has an intact, self-healing passive oxide layer.
Cr addition can improve oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance in a refractory HEA coating.
If wear removes oxide faster than it is regenerated, localized corrosion accelerates.
Accelerated localized corrosion increases total degradation.
Rapid oxide regeneration establishes a quasi-steady surface state that limits both wear and corrosion.
Simultaneous tribo-corrosion will produce a higher overall degradation rate than static corrosion of the same HEA.
Wear and corrosion will interact synergistically, producing a non-additive response relative to separate wear and corrosion tests.
A rapidly reformed oxide film may act as a lubricious layer and partially mitigate the wear component.
Static corrosive exposure without wear permits full development of a continuous passive oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism should apply preferentially to HEAs enriched in elements that enable fast oxide regeneration.
Low oxygen availability or extremely high wear rates can suppress oxide reformation enough for the proposed mechanism to fail or change markedly.
The quantitative partitioning of degradation into wear and corrosion components depends strongly on alloy composition and test parameters.
